questions.q: A primary source is
o: information you collect first-hand, e.g. a survey you run
questions.why: Secondary sources are others' work.

questions.q: The most reliable source on a medical claim is usually
questions.why: Peer review checks methods and evidence.

questions.q: Which is the best first step in research?
o: Write a clear question to investigate
questions.why: A focused question guides your sources.

questions.q: A student wants to find out how far students at their school travel each day. Which method would give the most useful data?
o: Reading a national newspaper article on transport
A short questionnaire given to a sample of students from every year group
Searching social media for posts about travel
questions.why: A questionnaire to a sample across all year groups gives first-hand data that represents the whole school.

questions.q: A student is researching plastic pollution in a local river. Which of these is a secondary source?
o: Their own count of plastic items on the riverbank
A government report on the river's water quality
An interview they carried out with a local fisherman
Photographs they took along the river
questions.why: A secondary source was produced by someone else; the other three are data the student collected first-hand.

long.q: A student wants to find out how much food is wasted at their school. Suggest a suitable method for gathering this information, and explain one strength and one weakness of your method. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: a suitable, specific method (e.g. weighing food left on plates in the canteen each day; a survey of students)
B1: method detailed enough to carry out (who, when, for how long, how it is recorded)
B1: a strength explained (e.g. weighing gives accurate first-hand data, not opinion)
B1: a weakness explained (e.g. one week may not be typical; students may not answer a survey honestly)

questions.q: A 'perspective' is
o: a point of view shaped by experience and values
questions.why: GP asks you to compare personal, local, national and global perspectives.

questions.q: What is a consequence?
o: A result or effect of an issue
questions.why: Explain links between causes, consequences and possible courses of action.

questions.q: Why consider different perspectives (personal, local/national, global)?
o: Issues affect people at different scales in different ways
questions.why: Compare them to reach a judgement.

questions.q: Many young people move from rural areas to cities to find work. Which of these is a consequence of this migration rather than a cause?
o: There are few jobs in rural areas
Rural villages are left with an ageing population
Rural schools offer a limited range of courses
questions.why: An ageing village population results from young people leaving; the other options are reasons why they leave.

questions.q: Which statement is written from a national perspective?
o: I am worried I will not find a job when I leave school.
Our country's youth unemployment rate has risen to 15% this year.
The factory in our town closed last month.
Youth unemployment is rising in many countries around the world.
questions.why: It describes the issue at the level of one country; the others are personal, local and global perspectives.

long.q: Explain two causes of increasing traffic congestion in many cities and one consequence of it, from either a local or a global perspective. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: first cause explained (e.g. rising car ownership as incomes grow, so more vehicles share the same roads)
B1: a second, different cause explained (e.g. poor or expensive public transport, so people choose to drive)
B1: a consequence identified (e.g. air pollution, longer journeys, lost working time)
B1: the consequence explained from the stated perspective (local: residents' health; global: emissions adding to climate change)

questions.q: A vested interest means
o: the author gains from persuading you
questions.why: e.g. a company reporting on its own product.

questions.q: How do you judge a source's reliability?
o: Check the author's expertise, purpose, evidence and date
questions.why: Bias and vested interest weaken reliability.

questions.q: What is a vested interest?
o: A personal stake that may bias a source
questions.why: For example a company writing about its own product.

questions.q: A study funded by a soft-drink company concludes that sugary drinks do not cause weight gain. What is the main reason to treat this source with caution?
o: It is about a health issue
The funder has a vested interest that may bias the findings
questions.why: The company gains if people believe its drinks are harmless, so the research may have been designed or reported to favour it.

questions.q: An article argues: 'Recycling is pointless, because my neighbour never bothers to recycle.' What is the main weakness of this argument?
o: It relies on too much statistical evidence
It generalises from a single personal example
It is written by an expert
questions.why: One neighbour's behaviour is not evidence about whether recycling as a whole is effective.

long.q: A source claims 'Electric cars will solve air pollution in cities'. Evaluate how convincing this claim is.
scheme: B1: identifies the claim and any evidence offered
B1: questions the source: author, purpose, vested interest
B1: weakness: pollution also from roads, tyres, industry, and electricity generation
B1: a reasoned judgement on how convincing it is

questions.q: Reflection in GP means
o: considering how your views and skills changed
questions.why: Reflect on what you learned and how.

questions.q: What should a personal reflection show?
o: How your thinking changed and what you learned
Only your opinion at the start
questions.why: Be specific about evidence that changed your mind.

questions.q: Which is reflective writing?
o: 'I first thought…, but the evidence on… made me reconsider because…'
questions.why: Reflection explains, not just describes.

questions.q: After a project on fast fashion, which statement best shows reflection on how the student's own perspective changed?
o: Fast fashion produces a large share of global carbon emissions.
Our group finished the project on time.
I used to buy cheap clothes without thinking, but learning about factory conditions has made me plan to buy fewer, longer-lasting items.
Everyone should stop buying new clothes.
questions.why: Reflection explains how and why the student's own views or behaviour changed as a result of the research.

questions.q: Which is the most useful reflection on the student's own teamwork skills?
o: I found it hard to speak up in meetings at first, so next time I will prepare my points in advance.
Our project was the best in the class.
questions.why: It identifies a specific weakness and sets out a realistic way to improve, which is what good reflection does.

questions.q: Good teamwork in the project means
o: agreeing roles and contributing to a shared outcome
questions.why: Collaboration is assessed.

questions.q: Why set roles in a team project?
o: So tasks are shared fairly and work is coordinated
questions.why: Evaluate how well the team worked.

questions.q: What is a good way to resolve disagreement in a team?
o: Discuss the evidence and agree a way forward
questions.why: Explain this in your reflection.

questions.q: In a team project, one member keeps missing deadlines. What is the most constructive first response?
o: Do their part without telling them
Report them to the teacher straight away
Talk with them to find out why and agree a realistic task and deadline
Remove their name from the project
questions.why: Discussing the problem openly keeps the member involved and solves the cause, which is the basis of good collaboration.

questions.q: Why might a team plan its project with a shared timeline showing a deadline for each task?
o: So that one person can control everything
So everyone knows what is due when and progress can be checked
So that the team does not need to discuss anything
So that the project takes longer
questions.why: A shared plan makes responsibilities and deadlines clear and lets the team spot problems early.

questions.q: A good written argument is
o: clear, structured and supported by evidence
questions.why: Structure and evidence persuade.

questions.q: What makes communication of an argument clear?
o: A logical structure with evidence for each point
questions.why: Know your audience.

questions.q: Why reference sources?
o: To show where evidence came from and let others check it
questions.why: Include author, title, date and link.

questions.q: Which sentence best supports a claim with evidence?
o: Phones are obviously bad for learning.
Phones are distracting and annoying in class.
Phones distract students: in our survey of 120 students, 70% said they check messages during lessons.
questions.why: It backs the claim with specific data and says where the data came from.

questions.q: A student is giving a presentation on saving water to a class of 8-year-olds. Which approach is most effective?
o: Reading a long report word for word
Using as much technical vocabulary as possible
Simple language, a clear structure and a few striking visuals
Including every fact the student found
questions.why: Effective communication is adapted to its audience; young children need clear, simple and visual information.

long.q: Write a short structured argument (about 150 words) on whether schools should ban mobile phones during lessons. Support your reasons with evidence, respond to another perspective, and reach a conclusion. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: a clear position stated at the start
B1: reasons supported by evidence or specific examples
B1: an opposing perspective acknowledged and answered
B1: a conclusion that follows from the reasoning, in clear, organised paragraphs
